title: SYSK Selects: Lying Liars: How Lying Works, Liar
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the June 2012 episode "Lying Liars: How Lying Works, Liar." Josh and Chuck explore what counts as a lie (Cecilia Bok's three-part definition, lies of omission, white lies), studies on children and lying, the Big Six motivations for lying, personality types prone to lying (pathological, compulsive, narcissistic, borderline, histrionic), body-language and micro-expression tells and why they are not reliable, a USC brain-structure study and TMS "thinking cap" research, and a study on how often people lie by medium (email, phone, text, in person). They also cover a five-step method for spotting lies and techniques liars use. The episode closes with listener mail about a teacher who used the earthworm episode with fourth graders, plus announcements about a horror fiction contest and Comic-Con.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the SYSK Selects episode, chosen from a June 2012 episode. The hosts banter about body language like blinking and face-touching, noting such behaviors are not necessarily signs of lying.

segments.title: Definition of a lie
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how common lying is according to studies, then present Cecilia Bok's philosophical definition of a lie: communicating information, intending to deceive, and believing the statement is false. They debate whether false information is required and whether lies of omission count.

segments.title: When lying is acceptable and white lies
segments.summary: The hosts discuss philosophers' view that lying is generally bad but has exceptions, such as lying to a murderer. They also discuss white lies told to spare feelings.

segments.title: Children and lying
segments.summary: Studies suggest children begin to lie around age two or three once they realize they are not constantly supervised. A study had kids told not to look at an object behind them, and older kids given a test with answers on the back who then lied about cheating. The hosts question the methodology and note the link to executive functioning and later success.

segments.title: The Big Six reasons people lie
segments.summary: Chuck lays out six motivations: concealing misdeeds, preserving reputation, white lies, increasing stature, manipulation, and controlling information. The hosts comment on each, including lies of cowardice and boastful people.

segments.title: Personality types prone to lying
segments.summary: The hosts describe the types most prone to lying: pathological liars (sociopathic, lie as strategy), compulsive liars (lie reflexively), narcissists, borderline personalities, and histrionic personalities, with an anecdote about a flight attendant.

segments.title: Nonverbal and verbal tells of lying
segments.summary: The hosts cover micro expressions, forced smiles, nodding during denial, defensive posture, fidgeting changes from baseline, and verbal cues such as taking too long, avoiding contractions, and repeating the question. They joke around a fictional example about a band gig.

segments.title: How liars sound convincing and a five-step method for catching lies
segments.summary: The hosts describe advice liars get: stay calm, keep it simple, remain steady, and be likable. They then outline a five-step method for spotting lies: establish a baseline, look for deviations, listen for details, use pauses, and change the subject. They mention the Colombo method.

segments.title: Brain structure, TMS, and lying by medium
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a USC study finding pathological liars have more white matter and less gray matter, and a TMS study where stimulating the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex increased lying. They also cover a study finding people lie least in email and most on the phone.

segments.title: Horror fiction contest and Comic-Con announcements
segments.summary: Announcements about a listener horror fiction contest with a June-July submission window and a live podcast at Comic-Con in San Diego on July 12.

segments.title: Listener mail: teacher using the earthworm episode
segments.summary: A fourth-grade teacher, Mr. Zach, reports that students listened to the earthworm podcast before dissecting earthworms, and most completed the questionnaire.
